original_question: Prove that the Riemann zeta function zeta(s) has at least one nontrivial zero rho = beta + i gamma whose positive imaginary part gamma is irrational.
target_in_paper: Theoretical problems, #1, Problem 1: "Prove that ζ(s) has at least one(!) irrational ordinate."
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper’s exact target. It correctly identifies the Riemann zeta function ζ(s), asks for an existence statement about a nontrivial zero, and focuses on the irrationality of a positive imaginary part.
missing_details: The paper’s official term is "ordinate," meaning the positive imaginary part of a nontrivial zero of the L-function.
To match the paper exactly, the question should be phrased as the existence of at least one irrational ordinate of ζ(s), not as a statement about a specific zero unless explicitly intended.
For a fully stand-alone formulation, one should make explicit that the zero is nontrivial, i.e. not one of the trivial zeros at the negative even integers.
The problem is unconditional; the paper does not assume RH, GRH, SZ, or LI in the statement.
The nearby Problem #2 ("Show that γ1 is irrational") is a stronger concrete special case, not the same problem as your draft.
The neighboring statement about positive ordinates not all being rational multiples of one another is a different, stronger problem and should not be merged into this question.
refined_question: Let an ordinate of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) mean the positive imaginary part of a nontrivial zero of ζ(s). Prove that ζ(s) has at least one irrational ordinate.
justification: The draft clearly targets the open problem in the paper’s section Theoretical problems, item #1, Problem 1, where the authors state exactly: "Prove that ζ(s) has at least one(!) irrational ordinate." On the same page, the paper defines an ordinate as a positive imaginary part of a nontrivial zero of an L-function, so the self-contained rewrite should import that definition directly. The nearby Problem #2, "Show that γ1 is irrational," is only presented as a concrete instance of the above problem and is therefore stronger than your draft, not an equivalent replacement. The introduction also confirms that the distribution of zeros and linear independence of their imaginary parts is one of the paper’s central themes, which is the broader context for this question. This paper does not contain a Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, or Theorem 1.3 relevant to your draft; the exact official formulation is the open problem above.
